It never talks to a KDC and never issues a ticket, so whose tickets it accepts is somebody else’s decision. The issuing half iskdc, and this module does not depend on it — see why they are separate.Ticket decryption is gokrb5’s.

Why it exists

gokrb5 is a client library. It verifies an AP-REQ and cannot build the AP-REP that answers one. Every GSS-API client asks for mutual authentication — MIT’s own gss-client sets GSS_C_MUTUAL_FLAG with no way to turn it off — so a service that cannot produce an AP-REP completes no context at all. Building it is most of what this module adds.

Example 

package main

import (
 "errors"
 "fmt"
 "log"

 "github.com/go-authn/krb5"
 "github.com/jcmturner/gokrb5/v8/keytab"
)

// establish is one GSS-API exchange: the client's AP-REQ in, the AP-REP out.
func establish(a *krb5.Acceptor, token []byte) (*krb5.Context, []byte, error) {
 ctx, apRep, err := a.Accept(token)
 if err != nil {
 return nil, nil, err // no context: refuse, never fall back to something weaker
 }
 // The client will not consider the context open until it has verified
 // apRep, so sending it back is not optional.
 log.Printf("%s (user %q, realm %q) until %s", ctx.Principal(), ctx.User(), ctx.Realm(), ctx.Expires())
 return ctx, apRep, nil
}

func main() {
 // In a service: krb5.Load("/etc/krb5.keytab", krb5.Principal("nfs/files.example.org")).
 // Here, an empty keytab, so the refusals can be seen.
 a := krb5.New(keytab.New(), krb5.Principal("nfs/files.example.org"))

 _, _, err := establish(a, []byte("not a token"))
 fmt.Println(errors.Is(err, krb5.ErrNotAToken), err)

 _, err = krb5.Load("/nonexistent/krb5.keytab")
 fmt.Println(errors.Is(err, krb5.ErrNoKeytab), err)
}
true krb5: not a GSS-API krb5 token: asn1: structure error: explicitly tagged member didn't match
true krb5: keytab "/nonexistent/krb5.keytab": open /nonexistent/krb5.keytab: no such file or directory

It needs github.com/jcmturner/gokrb5/v8 for keytab.New, which krb5.New takes; krb5.Load reads a keytab from a path instead.

After Accept, a *Context says who: Principal() (alice@EXAMPLE.ORG), orUser() and Realm() apart. Mapping a principal to a local account is the caller’s policy: alice@EXAMPLE.ORG and alice@PARTNER.ORG both answer to“alice”. Expires() is when the ticket behind it ends, past which a server holding a long-lived connection should stop honouring it. MIC/VerifyMIC and Wrap/Unwrap sign; Seal/Unseal add confidentiality (sec=krb5p).A Context is not safe for concurrent use; an Acceptor is.

What it refuses, and why

A ticket this service will not accept — wrong service, wrong key,expired, replayed, a clock beyond ClockSkew (five minutes by default, MIT’s too) — is ErrRejected. Bytes that are not a GSS-API krb5 token areErrNotAToken, and a token that is not an AP-REQ is ErrNotAPReq. The errors are deliberately coarse: a client learns that its ticket was refused, never which check refused it. An error means no context, and the returned token is empty.

A principal the acceptor does not answer for. Withkrb5.Principal("nfs/files.example.org"), a keytab holding several services answers for that one only.

A message whose signature does not match is ErrBadMIC, whichever of the length, the header, the sequence or the checksum disagreed. The acceptor signs with key usage 23 and verifies with 25, so a token this server produced cannot be replayed back at it as though the client had signed it.

A sealed token given to Unwrap is ErrSealed, distinct from a bad signature: a caller reading an integrity-only token must not be handed ciphertext that reads like a message. An unsealed token given to Unseal is ErrNotSealed: a protocol that promised confidentiality is not handed something that crossed the wire in the clear.

It asserts no acceptor subkey: the context key is the subkey the initiator put in its authenticator, or the ticket’s session key when it sent none(RFC 4121 §4.3).

A keytab is a secret at rest

Its path may come from a configuration file or from KRB5_KTNAME; the key inside it must never be logged, printed, or carried in an environment variable.

What it is checked against

A real MIT KDC and MIT’s own gss-client, against this package standing in for gss-server. test/kdc.sh builds a throwaway realm on loopback,unprivileged; the CI gets MIT Kerberos through pkgx (Ubuntu’s packages do not ship gss-client). The Linux test lane, the race detector and the coverage lane set KRB5_REQUIRE_JUDGE=1, so a missing fixture fails. A further step runs TestMITClientAgainstThisAcceptor and fails unless the log saysauthenticated as alice@ — a green lane whose judge silently stopped running is not accepted. TestMITClientSealed does the same with confidentiality on.

The macOS, Windows and cross-architecture lanes have no realm, and there the judge skips. The coverage lane’s floor is 90%.

Reference

pkg.go.dev/github.com/go-authn/krb5@v0.3.1

item.title: kdc — issuing Kerberos tickets from a directory
item.description:
How does a realm issue tickets from a directory? AS-REQ and TGS-REQ, over UDP and TCP, with encrypted-timestamp pre-authentication required, for the people a directory knows and the services a keytab holds. It runs underauthnd.

go get github.com/go-authn/kdc@v0.4.3

At v0.4.3 its go.mod requires at least go-authn/directory v0.12.0 and gokrb5 v8.4.4: minimums, so a program that requires directory v0.14.0, the version these pages describe, builds with v0.15.0, as authnd v0.13.0 does. The accepting half is krb5, and a service that only verifies tickets needs this module not at all.

Not implemented: cross-realm referrals, PKINIT, FAST, renewable or postdated tickets, and any kadmin protocol. Keys come from the directory and from a keytab, and change where they live.

Only a source holding the password can back a realm

A KDC must decrypt the client’s pre-authentication with that person’s long-term key, so a directory.Verifier — a bind against somebody else’s LDAP, a hash comparison — cannot serve, however well it answers is this the right password. A person whose source holds no password is answeredKDC_ERR_NULL_KEY (null key), never the code a wrong password gets, so it reads as a configuration to fix rather than a password to retype.

Example

A realm in memory, on loopback:

package main

import (
 "crypto/rand"
 "fmt"
 "log"
 "net"
 "time"

 "github.com/go-authn/directory"
 "github.com/go-authn/kdc"
 "github.com/jcmturner/gokrb5/v8/iana/etypeID"
 "github.com/jcmturner/gokrb5/v8/keytab"
)

func main() {
 // People: a source that holds PASSWORDS. A verifier cannot back a realm.
 people := &directory.Static{Name: "the configuration file", People: []*directory.Identity{
 directory.NewIdentity("alice", directory.WithPassword("correct horse battery staple")),
 }}

 // Services: the realm's own krbtgt key, and one per service.
 kt := keytab.New()
 for _, p := range []string{"krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG", "nfs/files.example.org"} {
 if err := kt.AddEntry(p, "EXAMPLE.ORG", rand.Text(), time.Now(), 1, etypeID.AES256_CTS_HMAC_SHA1_96); err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
 }
 }

 // A keytab without krbtgt/REALM is refused before anything listens.
 _, err := kdc.New(kdc.Config{Realm: "OTHER.ORG", People: people, Services: kt})
 fmt.Println(err)

 srv, err := kdc.New(kdc.Config{
 Realm: "EXAMPLE.ORG",
 People: people,
 Services: kt,
 Logf: log.Printf, // why each request was refused; never a key
 })
 if err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
 }
 pc, err := net.ListenPacket("udp", "127.0.0.1:18088")
 if err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
 }
 ln, err := net.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:18088")
 if err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
 }
 go srv.ServeTCP(ln)
 fmt.Println("EXAMPLE.ORG answers on", pc.LocalAddr())
 log.Fatal(srv.ServeUDP(pc))
}

With a krb5.conf naming kdc = tcp/127.0.0.1:18088 for EXAMPLE.ORG, the Heimdal kinit that macOS ships (1.5.1) gets a ticket-granting ticket, withKRB5_CONFIG=krb5.conf and KRB5CCNAME=FILE:cc:

$ kinit --password-file=STDIN alice@EXAMPLE.ORG < alice.pw
$ klist
Credentials cache: FILE:cc
Principal: alice@EXAMPLE.ORG
Issued Expires Principal
Oct 26 12:34:16 2026 Oct 26 22:34:16 2026 krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG@EXAMPLE.ORG
$ kinit --password-file=STDIN alice@EXAMPLE.ORG < bad.pw
kinit: Password incorrect
$ kinit --password-file=STDIN bob@EXAMPLE.ORG < alice.pw
kinit: krb5_get_init_creds: Error from KDC: no such principal in this realm
$ kgetcred nfs/files.example.org@EXAMPLE.ORG
$ klist
Credentials cache: FILE:cc
Principal: alice@EXAMPLE.ORG
Issued Expires Principal
Oct 26 12:34:16 2026 Oct 26 22:34:16 2026 krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG@EXAMPLE.ORG
Oct 26 12:34:16 2026 Oct 26 22:34:16 2026 nfs/files.example.org@EXAMPLE.ORG

The ten hours are Config.Lifetime’s default, and the service ticket ends with the ticket-granting ticket it was bought with. The KDC said why it refused each request, in its own log:

kdc: the keytab has no krbtgt key for this realm: matching key not found in keytab. Looking for "krbtgt/OTHER.ORG" realm: OTHER.ORG kvno: 0 etype: 18
EXAMPLE.ORG answers on 127.0.0.1:18088
2026/10/26 12:34:16 refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: pre-authentication required (code 25)
2026/10/26 12:34:16 refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: pre-authentication required (code 25)
2026/10/26 12:34:16 the timestamp does not decrypt (client etype 18, our key type 18): error decrypting: integrity verification failed
2026/10/26 12:34:16 refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: pre-authentication does not decrypt (code 24)
2026/10/26 12:34:16 refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: no such principal in this realm (code 6)

The first refusal of each exchange is the protocol working: the KRB-ERROR that demands pre-authentication carries an ETYPE-INFO2 hint naming the etype and the salt, and the client tries again with a timestamp.

Before v0.4.2, a till of 19700101000000Z got a ticket that had already expired

RFC 4120 §5.4.1: a till of 19700101000000Z asks for the maximum end time the KDC’s policy permits. Heimdal’s kgetcred sends exactly that. v0.4.1 tested only for Go’s zero time, so it took the Unix epoch for a real end and issued a service ticket that klist showed as >>>Expired<<<; MIT’s kvno,the CI’s judge, sends a real till and never met the case. v0.4.2 issues the longest ticket allowed, as above, and answers a till that has already passed with KDC_ERR_NEVER_VALID instead of a ticket expired on arrival(go-authn/kdc#19).

What it refuses, and why

At configuration (New): no realm (ErrNoRealm), no directory(ErrNoPeople), no keytab (ErrNoServices), or a keytab withoutkrbtgt/REALM@REALM (ErrNoTGTKey) — rather than starting and failing at the first kinit, where the error reaches a person who cannot fix it.

At the AS: a request without pre-authentication is answered with the demand for it, and the person’s key is not derived until there is a timestamp to check, so a spoofed UDP packet naming a real principal costs no key derivation. A wrong password, a timestamp under another etype and one from an hour ago are all answered KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED, the code a wrong password gets; the error text names the reason, and so does Logf. A service asking for a TGT of its own is refused: services authenticate from a keytab.

One encryption type. Tickets and keys are aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 (etype 18) only. A request whose etype list lacks 18 is answeredKDC_ERR_ETYPE_NOSUPP before anybody is looked up. With Logf set, the log records both etypes, so an operator can tell a mismatched cipher from a mistyped password.

At the TGS (RFC 4120 §3.3.2), a ticket is issued only when:

  • the ticket presented is a TGT of this realm, decrypted under thekrbtgt/REALM key the KDC names — not under the key of whatever service the ticket claims (KRB_AP_ERR_NOT_US);
  • the authenticator decrypts under its session key, within MaxSkew;
  • its checksum is over this request’s body, as the bytes arrived, keyed with the session key (KRB_AP_ERR_INAPP_CKSUM when missing or unkeyed,KRB_AP_ERR_MODIFIED when wrong);
  • the TGT is not past its end (KRB_AP_ERR_TKT_EXPIRED), not before its start and not flagged invalid (KRB_AP_ERR_TKT_NYV), with no skew allowed: this KDC’s clock wrote those times;
  • the client is of this realm and still in the directory(KDC_ERR_C_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN).

Lifetimes. Config.Lifetime caps a ticket, ten hours when zero; a client asking for less gets less, and a ticket bought with a TGT ends no later than that TGT, so asking for krbtgt again cannot stretch a credential.

What an unauthenticated peer can hold: a TCP message, its length included,must arrive within 30 seconds; at most 256 TCP connections are served at once,and at most 64 datagrams are answered at once — one more is dropped, and the client resends or falls back to TCP.

What it is checked against

MIT’s own kinit and kvno, through pkgx, against a realm built in Go —no MIT KDC is involved, only the client is borrowed.TestMITClientGetsATGTAndAServiceTicket gets a TGT and a service ticket and checks the key version kvno reports. The Linux test lane, the race detector and the coverage lane set KDC_REQUIRE_JUDGE=1, and a further step fails unless the log says were served by this realm. The tests also pin the refusals a real client never triggers: a timestamp under the wrong key, one from an hour ago, a three-byte cipher, a service asked for straight from an AS-REQ, a forged service ticket at the TGS, and a realm backed by a verifier.The coverage lane’s floor is 80%.

Reference

pkg.go.dev/github.com/go-authn/kdc@v0.4.3

item.title: oidc — verifying a bearer token
item.description:
Who does this bearer token say is asking, and should it be believed? Discovery, the key set, and the checks a resource server must make — in pure Go, with no dependencies outside the standard library.

go get github.com/go-authn/oidc@v0.4.1

There is no login flow here: no redirect, no code exchange, no client secret,no cookies. This is the resource-server half — something arrives with a token, and this says who that is.

Example 

package main

import (
 "context"
 "fmt"
 "log"
 "net/http"
 "strings"

 "github.com/go-authn/oidc"
)

func main() {
 // Discovery happens here, at startup: an issuer that does not answer is
 // a server that cannot authenticate anybody.
 v, err := oidc.New(context.Background(), oidc.Config{
 Issuer: "https://login.example.org",
 Audience: "fileshare",
 Type: "at+jwt", // a resource server takes access tokens, not ID tokens
 })
 if err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
 }

 http.HandleFunc("/", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
 raw, ok := strings.CutPrefix(r.Header.Get("Authorization"), "Bearer ")
 if !ok {
 http.Error(w, "unauthorized", http.StatusUnauthorized)
 return
 }
 tok, err := v.Verify(r.Context(), raw)
 if err != nil {
 log.Print(err) // which check refused it: for this log only
 http.Error(w, "unauthorized", http.StatusUnauthorized)
 return
 }
 fmt.Fprintln(w, tok.Subject(), tok.Username(), tok.Groups())
 })
 log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil))
}

A Verifier is safe for concurrent use and holds the key set: build one at startup and keep it. Verify’s error says which check refused the token, for the server’s log; the client gets one refusal whatever the check.

Three configurations New refuses before anything is fetched:

package main

import (
 "context"
 "fmt"

 "github.com/go-authn/oidc"
)

func main() {
 ctx := context.Background()
 for _, cfg := range []oidc.Config{
 {Issuer: "http://login.example.org", Audience: "fileshare"},
 {Issuer: "https://login.example.org"},
 {Audience: "fileshare"},
 } {
 _, err := oidc.New(ctx, cfg)
 fmt.Println(err)
 }
}
oidc: http://login.example.org is not https: the key set decides every signature, and over cleartext so does anybody on the way
oidc: no audience: a token minted for another service is a valid token, and a verifier that does not check accepts every one the issuer ever signed
oidc: no issuer: a verifier without one accepts tokens from anybody

The rest of Config is optional: JWKSURL skips discovery; UsernameClaim and GroupsClaim (default groups) name the claims; ClockSkew andMinRefresh default to one minute; Client is the HTTP client, for a proxy,a private CA or a timeout. A Token reads Subject, Issuer, Audience,Email, EmailVerified, Username, Groups, Expiry, NotBefore andIssuedAt; Claim(name, &v) decodes any other claim, and Has(name) says whether it is there.

What it accepts

Ten signature algorithms, as an allowlist: RS256 RS384 RS512,PS256 PS384 PS512, ES256 ES384 ES512, and EdDSA (Ed25519). A token whose alg is not one of these is refused before any key is fetched.alg: none and the HMAC family are refused by not being on the list, and the key must be of the algorithm’s kind: a token claiming RS256 is checked with an RSA key or refused.

What it refuses, and why

why
alg: none a token that says it is unsigned is a JSON object somebody typed
HMAC against a public key HS256 takes a shared secret, and the issuer’s key is public: anybody could mint a token
an issuer that merely starts with the right one iss is compared whole: https://login.example.org.evil.test starts with the right string
a missing or wrong audience a token minted for another service is valid; it is not addressed to this one
a token with no expiry it is a password somebody can copy once
an issuer, a key set, or a redirect over cleartext HTTP, except to loopback the key set decides every signature
an RSA key under 2048 bits, or with n or e not in shortest form; an EC point not on its curve signatures under a short key can be forged; before v0.2.2, a 1024-bit modulus padded with zero bytes passed as 2048 bits
a key published with use other than sig a key set legitimately holds encryption keys too
with Type set, a token of another typ; with it unset, a typ other than JWT or at+jwt (a token with no typ header passes) RFC 9068 §4: a resource server checks typ: at+jwt, or it takes an ID token for an access token whenever the audiences agree
a part that is not canonical base64url a token verifies as one string

ECDSA’s s and n − s both verify, as the algorithm allows. So a denylist or a replay cache keys on jti or sub, never on the token as sent.

Keys rotate, and an unknown key is not a way to hammer the issuer. A signature nothing held can verify is worth one refetch of the key set perMinRefresh, whether the kid is new or the same kid carries a new key.Tokens that need the key set while a fetch is under way wait for it, and a fetch that fails still counts.

Which name Username() gives. By default preferred_username, thenemail only when email_verified is true, then sub. An unverified email is a string the person typed (OIDC Core §5.1). A configured UsernameClaim is read as named, with no fallback.

What it is checked against

pyjwt signs every token in the test suite, so the verifier is never judged by a signer from the same hands. The HMAC-confusion token is forged by hand,because pyjwt refuses to produce it. testdata/fixed.json — tokens pyjwt signed once with a fixed key — lets the architecture lanes, s390x included,verify real signatures with the clock fixed. The Linux test lane, the race detector and the coverage lane install pyjwt and set OIDC_REQUIRE_JUDGE, so a missing pyjwt fails rather than skips. Accepting HMAC, comparing the issuer by prefix and skipping the audience check were each tried on purpose, and each turns a test red. The coverage lane’s floor is 90%.

Reference

pkg.go.dev/github.com/go-authn/oidc@v0.4.1

item.title: saml — a service provider in front of a federation
item.description:
What did this person’s identity provider say about them? A SAML 2.0 service provider for an identity federation such as RENATER’s Fédération Éducation-Recherche or eduGAIN: it reads the federation’s signed metadata,sends people to their own institution’s identity provider, and reads back what that provider says.

go get github.com/go-authn/saml@v0.5.0

It is the half of authn-bridge that faces the federation, and usable on its own by anything that wants to be a SAML SP. Not here: an IdP, Single Logout, the artifact binding, signed AuthnRequests, attribute queries, SAML 1.1.
Federation fetches the metadata, verifies it against a pinned certificate, and keeps it fresh with Run
ParseMetadata the same verification, for a document already in hand
DiscoveryURL, Chosen send the person to a discovery service, and read back the IdP it chose
SP.Request the AuthnRequest, over HTTP-Redirect, and the Pending to keep
SP.Accept the SAMLResponse posted to the ACS, read into an Assertion
Assertion.Subject subject-id, then pairwise-id, then eduPersonPrincipalName, then eduPersonTargetedID, then a persistent NameID — never mail
SP.Metadata the SP’s own metadata, to register with the federation

Example

Discovery and the request, with one IdP described by hand:

package main

import (
 "fmt"
 "net/url"

 "github.com/go-authn/saml"
)

func main() {
 // One IdP, as a federation's metadata would describe it.
 idp := &saml.IdP{
 EntityID: "https://idp.univ-example.example/idp/shibboleth",
 SSO: "https://idp.univ-example.example/idp/profile/SAML2/Redirect/SSO",
 Scopes: []string{"univ-example.example"},
 }
 md := &saml.Metadata{IdPs: map[string]*saml.IdP{idp.EntityID: idp}}

 sp := &saml.SP{
 EntityID: "https://app.example.org/saml",
 ACS: "https://app.example.org/saml/acs",
 Federation: md,
 }

 // Send the person to the discovery service, then read back what it chose.
 d, _ := saml.DiscoveryURL("https://discovery.renater.fr/renater", sp.EntityID, "https://app.example.org/saml/chosen")
 fmt.Println(d)

 _, err := saml.Chosen(url.Values{"entityID": {"https://idp.attacker.example/idp"}}, md)
 fmt.Println(err)
 chosen, _ := saml.Chosen(url.Values{"entityID": {idp.EntityID}}, md)

 // The AuthnRequest, over HTTP-Redirect. Keep p, keyed by the RelayState,
 // and hand it to sp.Accept at the ACS.
 to, p, err := sp.Request(chosen, "s1", saml.Options{AuthnContext: []string{"https://refeds.org/profile/mfa"}})
 if err != nil {
 panic(err)
 }
 u, _ := url.Parse(to)
 fmt.Println(u.Host, u.Query().Has("SAMLRequest"), u.Query().Get("RelayState"), p.IdP, p.AuthnContext)

 // RelayState is limited to 80 bytes, and refused beyond that.
 _, _, err = sp.Request(chosen, string(make([]byte, 81)), saml.Options{})
 fmt.Println(err)
}
https://discovery.renater.fr/renater?entityID=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.example.org%2Fsaml&return=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.example.org%2Fsaml%2Fchosen&returnIDParam=entityID
the chosen identity provider is not in the federation
idp.univ-example.example true s1 https://idp.univ-example.example/idp/shibboleth [https://refeds.org/profile/mfa]
RelayState is limited to 80 bytes

In a service, the metadata comes from the federation and the response arrives at the ACS:

package main

import (
 "context"
 "crypto/rsa"
 "crypto/tls"
 "crypto/x509"
 "encoding/pem"
 "log"
 "net/http"
 "os"

 "github.com/go-authn/saml"
)

func main() {
 ctx := context.Background()

 // The federation's metadata signing certificate, downloaded ONCE and
 // checked against the fingerprint the federation publishes.
 fed := &saml.Federation{
 URL: "https://pub.federation.renater.fr/metadata/fer/idps.xml",
 Cert: readCert("/etc/app/metadata-signature-2026.pem"),
 }
 if err := fed.Refresh(ctx); err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
 }
 go fed.Run(ctx, func(err error) { log.Print(err) })

 pair, err := tls.LoadX509KeyPair("/etc/app/saml.crt", "/etc/app/saml.key")
 if err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
 }
 sp := &saml.SP{
 EntityID: "https://app.example.org/saml",
 ACS: "https://app.example.org/saml/acs",
 Key: pair.PrivateKey.(*rsa.PrivateKey), // assertions arrive encrypted to it
 Cert: pair.Leaf,
 Federation: fed,
 }

 http.HandleFunc("/saml/acs", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
 p := pendingFor(r.PostFormValue("RelayState")) // what Request returned, from the session
 a, err := sp.Accept(r.PostFormValue("SAMLResponse"), p)
 if err != nil {
 log.Print(err) // for the log, not for the browser
 http.Error(w, "refused", http.StatusForbidden)
 return
 }
 id, from := a.Subject()
 log.Printf("%s (%s) from %s", id, from, a.IdP.EntityID)
 })
 log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServeTLS(":443", "/etc/app/tls.crt", "/etc/app/tls.key", nil))
}

func readCert(path string) *x509.Certificate {
 b, err := os.ReadFile(path)
 if err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
 }
 blk, _ := pem.Decode(b)
 if blk == nil {
 log.Fatal("no PEM block in ", path)
 }
 c, err := x509.ParseCertificate(blk.Bytes)
 if err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
 }
 return c
}

// pendingFor is the caller's session store.
func pendingFor(relayState string) saml.Pending { return saml.Pending{} }

What it refuses, and why

Metadata:

why
not signed by the pinned certificate the certificate is a parameter, never fetched alongside the metadata: a key that arrives over the same channel as the document vouches for nothing
past its validUntil, or with none a signed document that never expires is a key compromise that never ends. A failed refresh keeps the last good copy, until that copy expires
valid for more than 28 days from now Federation.MaxValidity changes the bound; a negative value removes it
older than the copy in use a rollback: validly signed, and possibly carrying a key since revoked
fetched over http:// from anywhere but loopback the signature would catch a change, but not a path that holds back the new document

An IdP’s certificate in metadata is trusted because the federation’s signature names it; its dates are not looked at, since IdP certificates are often self-signed and expired.

Responses are checked at Accept. Each refusal below is returned to the caller as an error, for the server’s log:

why
nothing signed, or signed with SHA-1 saml-profiles 4.1.4.5: over POST the assertion must be signed. A Shibboleth IdP signs the Response by default; either is accepted
more than one assertion how a signed one and an unsigned one arrive together and the wrong one is read (CVE-2022-41912)
anything outside what the signature covered it is never read: only the element rebuilt from the bytes the signature digested is
a scoped identifier outside the IdP’s Scopes dropped: otherwise any IdP could assert alice@another-university.example
AES-CBC ciphertext no verified signature covers not even decrypted: unauthenticated CBC is a padding oracle. RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 key transport is not accepted at all; AES-GCM and RSA-OAEP are
another audience, ACS or request; an unsolicited response; a request more than an hour old saml-profiles 4.1.4.3
an assertion already used a bearer assertion is whoever holds it
a condition it does not understand saml-core 2.5.1: the assertion is then Indeterminate
a password returned when MFA was asked for (Options.AuthnContext) an IdP may ignore the request
with ForceAuthn, an AuthnInstant from before the request the IdP reused a session it was asked not to

The default replay cache is one process’s memory

SP.Replay defaults to NewMemoryReplay(). Several instances behind a load balancer would each accept the same assertion once, and a restart empties it. Implement Replay over shared storage; its Use must be atomic.

Testing a program built on it: samltest

github.com/go-authn/saml/samltest (since v0.5.0) is a federation and an IdP for the tests of programs built on this package, such as an OpenID provider in front of a federation (go-authn/bridge) or what sits behind one (go-llmflow/bench). It is pure Go: xmlsec1 is not needed to use it.

fed, _ := samltest.NewParty("federation")
key, _ := samltest.NewParty("idp")
idp := &samltest.IdP{EntityID: "https://idp.univ-ex.example/idp/shibboleth",
 Scope: "univ-ex.example", SSO: srv.URL + "/SSO", Signer: key}
md, _ := (&samltest.Federation{Signer: fed, IdPs: []*samltest.IdP{idp}}).Metadata(24 * time.Hour)
// serve md; pin fed.Fingerprint() in the program's configuration
srv.Config.Handler = idp.Handler(spEntityID, acsURL, spCert, func(user, pw string) ([]samltest.Attribute, bool) {
 return []samltest.Attribute{{Name: samltest.EPPN, Values: []string{user + "@univ-ex.example"}},
 {Name: samltest.Entitlement, Values: []string{"grp-alpha"}}}, pw == "secret"
})
  • Metadata: an EntitiesDescriptor signed by the federation’s key, with each IdP’s scope, display name, signing certificate and HTTP-Redirect SSO location.
  • Responses: IdP.Response takes an Assertion with the request ID, audience,ACS and attributes. The Response is signed with RSA-SHA256, exclusive c14n,enveloped, after the Issuer. The assertion is encrypted to the SP’s certificate with AES-128-GCM and RSA-OAEP MGF1-SHA1 (a Shibboleth IdP v5’s defaults), or signed itself in the clear when EncryptTo is nil.
  • The login: IdP.Handler shows a username and password form for an AuthnRequest and answers with the form that posts SAMLResponse and RelayState to the ACS; a test’s HTTP client submits it as a browser’s script would.

Its output is judged by parties that did not write it: xmlsec1 verifies the metadata and both kinds of Response and decrypts the assertion (that test skips where xmlsec1 is absent, and says so; with SAML_REQUIRE_JUDGE=1 it fails instead), and this package’s SP accepts them and refuses them tampered, replayed or signed by a key the federation does not list. The keys are generated per call, so nothing here belongs in production.

What it is checked against

  • RENATER’s own metadata, as RENATER signed it on 2026-09-29, intestdata/fer-idps.xml.gz, with its certificate checked against the SHA-256 fingerprint RENATER publishes. All 343 IdPs are read; rewriting the host of one Location is refused. The architecture lanes, s390x included,verify that signature too.
  • xmlsec1 signs and encrypts every response in the suite, from templates:GCM and CBC, RSA-OAEP with SHA-1 and with SHA-256, Response signed,assertion signed, both. The Linux test lane, the race detector and the coverage lane install it and set SAML_REQUIRE_JUDGE.
  • crewjam/saml’s IdP writes whole responses to this SP’s AuthnRequests in a separate CI job (interop/crewjam, a module of its own, not in the published module): RSA-SHA256 with AES-128-CBC and the Response signed is accepted; its default RSA-SHA1 is refused; the same CBC assertion with the Response signature removed is refused before decryption.

The coverage lane’s floor is 92%.

item.title: krl — OpenSSH key revocation lists
item.description:
Is this SSH certificate or key revoked — as sshd would answer? The binary format of OpenSSH’s PROTOCOL.krl, the list sshd loads throughRevokedKeys and ssh-keygen -k writes. golang.org/x/crypto/ssh has no support for it.

go get github.com/go-authn/krl@v0.6.1

IsRevoked follows ssh_krl_check_key in OpenSSH’s krl.c: a certificate is revoked when its serial or key ID is revoked under the CA that signed it or under any CA, when its CA key is revoked, or when its own key is revoked by blob or by SHA-1 or SHA-256 fingerprint. Serial 0 — what a CA writes when it names none — is never revoked by serial.

Example 

package main

import (
 "crypto/ed25519"
 "crypto/rand"
 "fmt"
 "time"

 "github.com/go-authn/krl"
 "golang.org/x/crypto/ssh"
)

func main() {
 ca := signer()
 user := signer()

 // The issuer: certificate 42 is revoked, and so is everything for key ID "alice".
 b := krl.NewBuilder(7, "revoked by the bridge")
 b.RevokeSerial(ca.PublicKey(), 42)
 b.RevokeKeyID(nil, "alice") // nil: under any CA
 b.SetExpires(time.Now().Add(time.Hour))
 data, err := b.Marshal(time.Now())
 if err != nil {
 panic(err)
 }

 // The server: parse the list, then ask about each certificate.
 k, err := krl.Parse(data)
 if err != nil {
 panic(err)
 }
 fmt.Println("version", k.Version, "signed", k.Signed, "expires set", !k.Expires.IsZero())
 for _, c := range []struct {
 serial uint64
 id string
 }{{42, "bob"}, {43, "bob"}, {44, "alice"}} {
 fmt.Println(c.serial, c.id, k.IsRevoked(certificate(ca, user.PublicKey(), c.serial, c.id)))
 }
}

func signer() ssh.Signer {
 _, priv, _ := ed25519.GenerateKey(rand.Reader)
 s, _ := ssh.NewSignerFromKey(priv)
 return s
}

func certificate(ca ssh.Signer, key ssh.PublicKey, serial uint64, id string) *ssh.Certificate {
 c := &ssh.Certificate{
 Key: key, Serial: serial, KeyId: id, CertType: ssh.UserCert,
 ValidPrincipals: []string{id}, ValidBefore: ssh.CertTimeInfinity,
 }
 if err := c.SignCert(rand.Reader, ca); err != nil {
 panic(err)
 }
 return c
}
version 7 signed false expires set true
42 bob true
43 bob false
44 alice true

The same list and certificates, written to files, get the same three answers from OpenSSH 10.3p1’s ssh-keygen -Q -f list.krl: REVOKED, ok,REVOKED.

Expiry: expires@go-authn.github.io

A KRL has a generation date and a version, and nothing says when it stops being current, so a stale copy cannot be told from a fresh one.Builder.SetExpires writes that time in an extension section namedExtensionExpires, not critical, so sshd and ssh-keygen load the list and ignore it; Parse reads it into KRL.Expires.

No signatures

OpenSSH never exposed a way to write the KRL signature section and no longer verifies it. Parse skips one and sets Signed, which says nothing about authenticity; Builder never writes one. The list’s integrity, and so its expiry’s, comes from its transport — HTTPS from an authenticated server — or from a detached SSHSIG signature checked by the caller, which this package does not do.

Merging: one file for sshd

sshd read a single RevokedKeys file until OpenSSH 10.3, so a server trusting several CAs needs their lists in one. Builder.Merge adds every revocation of a parsed list. Builder.MergeCA(k, ca, others...) keeps k’s section for ca, its any-CA sections re-scoped to ca, and its explicit keys and fingerprints, and leaves out — counting them — sections for another CA and keys or fingerprints that designate one of others. MergeCAWith withMergeOptions{DropKeys: true} also leaves out every explicit key exceptca’s own, for a list not trusted with every CA’s users: a revoked user key locks that user out under every CA of the merged file, because sshd checks a certificate’s own key whoever signed it.

What it refuses, and why

Parse refuses what ssh-keygen and sshd refuse: a bad magic or format version, truncated or trailing data, an unknown section or certificate subsection, an unknown extension marked critical, a CA key OpenSSH cannot parse, serial 0, an inverted serial range, a bitmap larger than OpenSSH reads or one that wraps past 2^64−1. It also refuses a malformed or repeated expiry:read as absent, it would turn a list meant to lapse into one that never does.

Builder refuses — at Marshal, which returns the first invalid request —serial 0, a range whose low end is 0 or above its high end, a key ID or comment containing a NUL, a certificate given where a CA key is expected, and an expiry before the generation date.

One deliberate difference. For many sparse serials close together,ssh-keygen -k writes a bitmap wider than its own reader accepts and then refuses its own file (bignum is too large). Parse refuses that file too,as sshd would; Builder starts a new section before a bitmap gets that wide, so what it writes is always readable.

Parse allocates in proportion to what the list revokes, as OpenSSH does: a KRL should come from a source trusted not to send an enormous one.

What it is checked against

OpenSSH’s ssh-keygen, on the Linux and macOS lanes, whereKRL_REQUIRE_SSHKEYGEN=1 makes a missing one a failure (Windows runs the pure-Go tests only):

  • a KRL written by ssh-keygen -k with every serial encoding, key IDs, three CAs plus “any CA”, explicit keys and a revoked CA key: IsRevoked answers like ssh-keygen -Q for 250 certificates, and Builder given the same revocations writes the same bytes;
  • 40 random serial sets written by both: byte-identical, and the same answers for about 9000 certificates;
  • every truncation and about 1400 single-byte corruptions: Parse refuses exactly what ssh-keygen refuses;
  • the expiry extension loads in ssh-keygen, and the same section marked critical is refused;
  • merged lists revoke exactly what one of their sources revokes.

FuzzParse, seeded with KRLs ssh-keygen wrote, and FuzzBuilder run in CI.The coverage floor is 100%, measured on the Linux lane where ssh-keygen is present.

Reference

pkg.go.dev/github.com/go-authn/krl@v0.6.1

item.title: servercert — where a daemon's TLS certificate comes from
item.description:
Where does a daemon’s TLS server certificate come from? A certificate and key on disk, re-read when they change, or an ACME CA throughautocert, External Account Binding included.

go get github.com/go-authn/servercert@v0.5.2

A Config names exactly one source — CertFile and KeyFile, or ACME —and New returns a *Source whose TLSConfig() serves it, withMinVersion TLS 1.2.

Example

From files:

package main

import (
 "log"
 "net/http"

 "github.com/go-authn/servercert"
)

func main() {
 src, err := servercert.New(servercert.Config{
 CertFile: "/etc/fileshare/tls/fullchain.pem",
 KeyFile: "/etc/fileshare/tls/privkey.pem",
 OnError: func(err error) { log.Print(err) }, // a renewal that did not load
 })
 if err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err) // unreadable, unparsable, or a key that is not the certificate's
 }
 srv := &http.Server{Addr: ":443", TLSConfig: src.TLSConfig()}
 log.Fatal(srv.ListenAndServeTLS("", ""))
}

Config.Check refuses a configuration that cannot work, and touches nothing —no file read, no directory created:

package main

import (
 "fmt"

 "github.com/go-authn/servercert"
)

func main() {
 // Check touches nothing: no file is read, no directory created.
 for _, c := range []servercert.Config{
 {ACME: &servercert.ACME{Domains: []string{"*.example.org"}, CacheDir: "/var/lib/fileshare/acme"}},
 {ACME: &servercert.ACME{Domains: []string{"192.0.2.10"}, CacheDir: "/var/lib/fileshare/acme"}},
 {ACME: &servercert.ACME{Domains: []string{"files.example.org"}, CacheDir: "acme"}},
 {CertFile: "/etc/fileshare/tls/fullchain.pem"},
 {ACME: &servercert.ACME{Domains: []string{"files.example.org"}, CacheDir: "/var/lib/fileshare/acme",
 DirectoryURL: "http://acme.example.org/directory"}},
 {ACME: &servercert.ACME{Domains: []string{"files.example.org"}, CacheDir: "/var/lib/fileshare/acme"}},
 } {
 fmt.Println(c.Check())
 }
}
servercert: ACME domain "*.example.org" is a wildcard; that needs dns-01, which autocert does not do
servercert: ACME domain "192.0.2.10" is an IP address; autocert issues only for DNS names
servercert: ACME.CacheDir "acme" is not an absolute path
servercert: CertFile and KeyFile go together; one of them is empty
servercert: ACME.DirectoryURL "http://acme.example.org/directory" is not an https URL (RFC 8555 §6.1)
<nil>

The last one is Let’s Encrypt production: DirectoryURL empty.

Files

New reads the pair and fails now on one that is unreadable, does not parse, or whose key is not the certificate’s. After that, at most once every 10 seconds and during a handshake, the files are read again; a changed pair is parsed without holding a lock and swapped in. A changed pair that does not load — the certificate written before its key, a truncated file — is reported once to OnError, and the last good pair stays in service, so a renewal job that writes the two files one after the other never takes the server down.

ACME

autocert answers two challenge types and no other: tls-alpn-01 (RFC 8737,port 443, ALPN acme-tls/1) and, with HTTPChallenge, http-01 (RFC 8555§8.3, port 80, served by Source.HTTPHandler). There is no dns-01, hence no wildcard and no IP-address certificate.

Certificates are obtained at the first handshake whose SNI names one ofDomains, or before any client by Source.Prefetch, and renewed by autocert before they expire. A client that connects by IP address sends no SNI and is served the first domain’s certificate.

Append to NextProtos, never replace it

With ACME, TLSConfig().NextProtos holds acme-tls/1, without which the CA’s tls-alpn-01 validation fails. And append you must: a Go TLS server that advertises ALPN protocols refuses a client whose offer shares none, so an NFS-over-TLS server adds sunrpc (RFC 9289). net/http adds http/1.1 andh2 itself.

A CA that needs no challenge. autocert returns at once when a new order is already ready, which is what a CA with pre-validated domains answers: GÉANT TCS, served by HARICA, for an Enterprise Admin account. An internal server reachable on neither port 80 nor 443 from the Internet can still get a publicly trusted certificate. The EAB HMAC key is a secret, so the configuration names a file holding it (EABHMACKeyFile), never the key.

One defect of x/crypto/acme is worked around (golang/go#77704):after finalizing an order the CA is still processing, the client polls the URL in the finalize response’s Location header, which RFC 8555 does not put there. servercert gives the ACME client a transport that adds that header, with the order’s URL from the earlier newOrder response.

What it refuses, and why

Check refuses: neither or both sources; half a file pair; ACME without domains or cache directory; a relative path; half an EAB; a domain that is an IP address, a wildcard, a single label, ends with a dot, or is not a valid host name; a directory URL that is not https (RFC 8555 §6.1).

New also refuses a cache directory — it holds private keys — that is a symbolic link, is accessible by group or others, is owned by a user other than the process’s effective user, or cannot be written; a missing one is created0700 and checked after. Every directory above it must be changeable only by root or the effective user, as sshd’s StrictModes asks of the path toauthorized_keys, and a symbolic link above it is refused unless root owns it.On Windows, mode and owner are not checked — ACLs decide both, and restricting them is yours — and a symbolic link anywhere in the path is refused.

What it is checked against

pebble, Let’s Encrypt’s test CA, run in-process from its ca, db, va and wfe packages with a DNS stub, issuing real certificates that crypto/tls verifies against pebble’s root: tls-alpn-01; http-01 through HTTPHandler and its control with HTTPChallenge off; EAB required, absent, wrong, then right;a pre-validated domain issued with no challenge port open, and its control. A test runs the same issuance without the golang/go#77704 workaround and requires it to fail. The coverage floor is 100%.

Reference

pkg.go.dev/github.com/go-authn/servercert@v0.5.2

item.title: wireguard — whose key is this, and may it connect?
item.description:
May this WireGuard key connect, and whose is it? WireGuard authenticates a peer by its static public key and by nothing else: no certificates, no expiry,no revocation. So the question is answered outside the protocol, and answered again whenever the answer changes. A provider —authn-bridge — answers it; this module is what the provider and a gateway agree on.

go get github.com/go-authn/wireguard@v0.1.1

Its one dependency is oidc v0.4.0,which verifies the list.

It does two things: ParseKey says what a public key is, and Source.Fetch gets the provider’s signed List of the keys people registered, each a Peer with its Key, Subject, Username, Device and the end of its lease.

Only public keys pass through here

A private key is generated on the device and never leaves it; nothing in this package has a place for one.

Example 

package main

import (
 "crypto/ecdh"
 "encoding/base64"
 "fmt"
 "strings"

 "github.com/go-authn/wireguard"
)

func main() {
 // A public key as wg(8) prints it. Here it is derived from a fixed
 // private key; on a device, `wg genkey | wg pubkey` makes one, and the
 // private half never leaves it.
 priv, _ := ecdh.X25519().NewPrivateKey([]byte(strings.Repeat("\x2a", 32)))
 text := base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString(priv.PublicKey().Bytes())

 k, err := wireguard.ParseKey(text)
 fmt.Println(k, err)

 // The all-zero key authenticates nobody.
 _, err = wireguard.ParseKey(base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString(make([]byte, 32)))
 fmt.Println(err)

 // Unpadded is another spelling of the same bytes, and is refused.
 _, err = wireguard.ParseKey(strings.TrimRight(text, "="))
 fmt.Println(err)
}
B6r/Pp/BZydVRPTDpqF82Dfy7G54zYpXsePfs8wDWnY= <nil>
wireguard: the key is a point of low order, which authenticates nobody
wireguard: the key is not base64: illegal base64 data at input byte 40

A gateway keeps one Source and fetches the list:

package main

import (
 "context"
 "log"
 "os"
 "time"

 "github.com/go-authn/wireguard"
)

func main() {
 ctx := context.Background()
 src, err := wireguard.NewSource(ctx, wireguard.SourceConfig{
 Issuer: "https://bridge.example.org",
 ClientID: "gateway-1",
 ClientSecret: readSecret("/etc/gateway/client-secret"),
 })
 if err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
 }
 for {
 l, err := src.Fetch(ctx) // signed, typ wireguard-peers+jwt, for this gateway, not older
 if err != nil {
 log.Print(err)
 } else {
 for _, p := range l.Peers {
 log.Printf("peer %s is %s (%s) until %s", p.Key, p.Subject, p.Username, p.Expires)
 }
 }
 time.Sleep(time.Minute)
 }
}

// readSecret reads the client secret from a file: never from the command
// line or the environment.
func readSecret(path string) string {
 b, err := os.ReadFile(path)
 if err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
 }
 return string(b)
}

NewSource reads the provider’s configuration at startup. Fetch gets a token for the gateway itself (client_credentials, scope wireguard_peers),fetches the list from /wireguard/peers under the issuer, and verifies it with go-authn/oidc: the signature against the provider’s key set, the issuer,the audience (this gateway’s ClientID), the expiry, and the typ wireguard-peers+jwt (ListType) — so neither an access token nor an ID token can pass for a list, nor a list for a token.

What it refuses, and why

A key (ParseKey):

  • any other spelling of the same bytes. The decoding is strict and the text must print back exactly as it came, so a store keyed on the text cannot hold one key twice under two names;
  • a point of low order, the all-zero key among them. Every exchange with one gives the same shared secret whatever the other side’s key (RFC 7748 §6.1),so it authenticates nobody. crypto/ecdh decides it by computing an exchange, so the top-bit variants are refused too.

A list (Fetch):

why
a list with a lower version than one this Source has taken an old list is signed too, and may list a key taken back since
a key listed twice whichever a gateway kept, the other person’s traffic would arrive under the wrong name
a peer with no subject it belongs to nobody
a key that is not one see above
an issuer or token endpoint in the clear, except loopback the gateway’s secret and the list would cross a link anybody can read
a SourceConfig without ClientID and ClientSecret a gateway reads the list as a client of its own

A list carries exp: a gateway that cannot fetch a newer one by then has no list, rather than a stale one. Peer.Subject is the person’s sub as the client that registered the key sees it, public or pairwise — the value a gateway also finds in that person’s access tokens.

What it is checked against

wg(8) itself, from wireguard-tools, makes the keys ParseKey must accept. It is installed in the Linux test lane, the race detector and the coverage lane, which set WIREGUARD_REQUIRE_JUDGE=1 so a missing wg fails rather than skips. The low-order test checks the seven points libsodium lists,each with and without the top bit. The coverage floor is 100%.

Reference

pkg.go.dev/github.com/go-authn/wireguard@v0.1.1

item.title: scim — provisioning people and groups from an identity provider
item.description:
Who has the identity provider just created, changed or deleted? An identity provider (Entra ID, Okta, Keycloak, …) creates, updates and deletes people and groups in your application over HTTP; this package is that HTTP endpoint, for Users and Groups (RFC 7643, RFC 7644), over a Backend you write. Pure Go, CGO_ENABLED=0, standard library only.

go get github.com/go-authn/scim@v0.1.0

Example 

srv := &scim.Server{
 Backend: scim.NewMemory(), // or your database
 BaseURL: "https://app.example.org/scim/v2", // for meta.location
}
mux.Handle("/scim/v2/", http.StripPrefix("/scim/v2", scim.BearerAuth(token, srv)))

The Server assigns ids, timestamps and versions, validates input and applies PATCH; the Backend keeps what it is given and enforces what only it can see:ErrConflict for a taken userName (409 uniqueness), InvalidValue for a member that does not exist (400 invalidValue), ErrPrecondition when the stored version is not the one that was read. NewMemory() is the reference implementation.

It serves /Users and /Groups (list with filter, startIndex, count,attributes, excludedAttributes; create; get, PUT, PATCH and DELETE by id with ETag and If-Match), /Users/.search and /Groups/.search, and the discovery endpoints /ServiceProviderConfig, /ResourceTypes and /Schemas.Filters cover the whole grammar of RFC 7644 §3.4.2.2; PATCH is atomic: an operation that fails leaves the resource as it was.

What it refuses, and why

Everything here comes from outside, so the limits are part of the API:
a body over MaxBodyBytes (1 MiB), a PATCH with more than MaxOperations (100), or one that grows the resource past the body limit 413
a group with more than MaxMembers (10 000) 400 invalidValue
a filter over 4 KiB, nested deeper than 32, with an unknown operator, or gt on a boolean 400 invalidFilter
writes to id, meta, schemas or a user’s groups 400 mutability
a resource without its core schema, a userName that is empty, over 256 bytes or has control characters, two primary emails 400
a missing or wrong bearer token (BearerAuth, constant time; an empty token admits nobody) 401
any Backend error that is not one of the sentinels 500 with a body that says nothing; the error goes to ErrorLog

Not supported: bulk operations, sorting, password changes, /Me (announced as such in /ServiceProviderConfig).

What it is checked against

What identity providers really send, tested with their payloads: Entra ID’s "Replace", its string booleans ("active": "False"), its member removal by value list, its filtered add that creates an email; Okta’s replace without a path that repeats the id. The filter, PATCH and the whole handler are fuzzed(FuzzFilter, FuzzPatch, FuzzServer), and the coverage lane’s floor is 92%.

Reference

pkg.go.dev/github.com/go-authn/scim@v0.1.0
